cells.tense: You're in the middle of it right now — deciding what the young thing needs today and giving it that, without hand-wringing.
cells.ask: Tell one person close to this what you've been keeping steady. Saying it where it can be heard is what lets someone hand something back.
cells.core: There's a plant on the windowsill and you know when it needs water and when it wants to be left alone. You keep the light right, you keep the water at the right amount, and you don't pull on the stem to hurry it. That steady attention is real work, whether or not anyone walks in and remarks on it. The looking-after is the accomplishment, not the bloom.\n\nSome of what you're owed hasn't been said — it reads as no big deal, just maintenance, just keeping things going — and the ease you feel at being nearly finished doesn't quite get named. Tell one person, out loud, that this work has been yours. What arrives isn't applause; it's a stone set under the next thing you plant.
cells.sheetLine: You keep the light right, and the plant grows because of it.
cells.verb: tending what's growing with responsible care
cells.place: in the part of life that looks after what's still coming up

cells.tense: You're already at the harvest in your head, and the season that's actually here hasn't finished growing.
cells.ask: Pick one thing that's growing and doing fine, and leave it alone for the whole evening. See whether it does the same thing on its own that you would have done to it.
cells.core: You mean well — you're trying to get ahead of trouble, to lay out the next three meals, the next three conversations, the next three months, so nothing has a chance to go wrong. That thoroughness is love, and it does keep things safe. But the care has gotten ahead of what's actually growing, and pulling on a shoot to hurry it stretches the shoot, not the season.\n\nThe way back is the act Fulfillment describes: the vision comes out of what's already happened, not out of what you're afraid hasn't happened yet. Let one thing run on its own tonight. If it comes out fine, you have a fact to trust. If it comes out differently than you'd have steered it, you have a fact there too. Either way you wake up with something the day actually did, instead of what you'd planned for it.
cells.sheetLine: You're pulling at the shoot, not the season.

cells.tense: You've been standing past a door for a while — the one where you used to actually do this — and you haven't gone back through.
cells.ask: Go water one real thing — a plant, a person, an unfinished task — and stop after five minutes without doing anything else about it.
cells.core: You know how to do this. That hasn't gone anywhere; the watering can is still by the sink. But the last stretch of life has pulled your hands off it, and now you don't quite reach — you watch other people tend their things and think, they've got it.\n\nThere's a way this looks when it's working: the small ordinary acts get done and the growing happens quietly around them. Water one plant this week, check on one person, finish one small unfinished thing. Don't decide whether it counts. Do the small act and let the doing be enough. What Resilience describes is keeping on after everything that's happened; it isn't enthusiasm, it's the next right thing. You don't have to feel like a gardener first. Put your hand on one stem and stay there for a minute. That's the rest of it.
cells.sheetLine: The watering can is still by the sink. Pick it up.

cells.tense: You're keeping something alive and calling it the thing that keeps itself alive, and what you're doing sits just off the edge of your own attention.
cells.ask: Say out loud, once, to someone: this is mine. About the one piece of growing you speak of as the situation's, or as just how it is.
cells.core: You already keep this alive. You notice what the day needs and you do it — the other person's mood gets eased, the plants get watered, the thing that's been falling apart gets propped up — and you're doing it so naturally that you're not calling it what it is. There's nothing shameful in a talent you haven't sat down and named.\n\nWhat Honor describes is making the intent visible, from the inside first, so the looking-after stops being something you owe and starts being something you hold. Put the claim back where it belongs. Say the sentence to one person who has watched you do it: this is mine. Not in a boast — in a handoff. You'll know which piece. It's been waiting for you to say it.
cells.sheetLine: You're the one keeping it alive. Say so.

The sentence that serves me most is the Too Much opening about pushing the season; it's the one I'd keep because I like the sound of it, so I've leaned on it least and made it do work instead of decoration.
